title: Xcode, Swift Package Manager & Project Structure
scopeHtml: Scope: Xcode project anatomy, targets, schemes, build configurations, xcconfig, SPM, modularization, Info.plist, assets, Gradle comparison.

notes.title: Baseline and the Xcode vs Gradle map
notes.html:
Android equivalent. An Android project is Gradle: settings.gradle, a root build.gradle, module build.gradle(.kts) files, buildTypes, productFlavors, AndroidManifest.xml, res/. In iOS (Xcode 16+, Swift 6 mode, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first) the equivalents are an .xcodeproj (or .xcworkspace), targets, schemes, build configurations, Info.plist, asset catalogs, and Swift Package Manager (SPM).

Baseline. Swift Package Manager is the default dependency tool. CocoaPods and Carthage are legacy that you will meet in old codebases. Xcode 16 introduced synchronized folder groups (file-system based project groups, verify in your version), which reduce merge conflicts in project.pbxproj.

Android / Gradle iOS / Xcode
Project (settings.gradle) Workspace (.xcworkspace)
Module (:app, :feature:home) Target (app, framework, test bundle) or SPM package/target
buildTypes (debug, release) Build Configuration (Debug, Release, custom)
productFlavors Targets, schemes + xcconfig, or build configurations
Run configuration Scheme
build.gradle dependencies Package.swift / Xcode package dependencies
AndroidManifest.xml Info.plist + entitlements
res/ Asset catalog, string catalog, storyboards
gradle.properties, local.properties .xcconfig files
./gradlew build xcodebuild
~/.gradle/caches, build/ DerivedData
Signing config (keystore) Signing & provisioning profiles, certificates
Gradle sync Package resolution 
 MyApp.xcworkspace
 |-- MyApp.xcodeproj
 |     |-- Target: MyApp            (app)
 |     |-- Target: MyAppTests       (unit tests)
 |     |-- Target: MyAppUITests
 |     |-- Target: MyWidget         (extension)
 |     |-- Build Configurations: Debug, Release, Staging
 |     `-- Schemes: MyApp, MyApp-Staging, MyWidget
 `-- Packages/
       |-- Core        (local SPM package)
       |-- Networking
       `-- FeatureHome

Analogy. Xcode is a workshop: the workspace is the building, projects are rooms, targets are the products being built, and schemes are the job tickets telling the workshop which product to build and how to run it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying scheme equals build variant. A scheme selects a target and a configuration for each action (Run, Test, Archive); a configuration is the set of build settings.
  • Calling a workspace a "bigger project"; it is a container that groups projects and packages so they build together.
  • Assuming Xcode projects are text-diffable. project.pbxproj is a generated-looking plist that conflicts in merges (hence XcodeGen, Tuist, synchronized groups).

notes.title: Project anatomy: targets, schemes, configurations
notes.html:
Android equivalent. A module with a com.android.application plugin is the app; buildTypes and productFlavors multiply variants like stagingDebug. In Xcode these three concepts are separate.

Target. One product to build, with its own sources, resources, build settings, Info.plist and dependencies. Product types: App, Framework / static library, App Extension (widget, share, notification service), Unit Test bundle, UI Test bundle, App Clip, Watch app. Each extension is its own target and is embedded into the app target.

Build Configuration. A named set of build settings. Default: Debug and Release. Debug turns off optimization (-Onone) and enables debug info; Release uses -O or -Osize, whole module optimization, strips symbols. You can duplicate to add Staging.

Scheme. A recipe that says: for action Run use target X with configuration Debug; for Test use test targets Y; for Archive use Release. Schemes are shared (checked into xcshareddata/xcschemes) or personal (xcuserdata, ignored by git). CI uses xcodebuild -scheme MyApp, so a scheme must be marked Shared or CI cannot see it: a classic CI failure ("scheme not found").

xcodebuild -list
xcodebuild -workspace MyApp.xcworkspace -scheme MyApp-Staging \
  -configuration Staging -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16' build
xcodebuild test -scheme MyApp -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16'

Build phases (per target). Compile Sources, Link Binary With Libraries, Copy Bundle Resources, Embed Frameworks, Run Script. Custom run scripts (SwiftLint, code gen, Crashlytics dSYM upload) go in Run Script phases. In Xcode 15+ with ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING = YES scripts need declared inputs/outputs or they fail with "Sandbox: deny file-read".

Build settings levels (cascade).

 Platform defaults < Project-level settings < xcconfig (project) < Target-level settings < xcconfig (target)
 (target overrides project; settings in the UI use $(inherited) to inherit)

Mapping product flavors. Choose per need:

  • Staging vs production backend: build configurations + xcconfig + Info.plist values (next section).
  • Different app identity (white label, different icon/bundle id installed side by side): extra target or scheme + configuration with a different PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER.
  • Free vs paid versions: usually a single target with feature flags / StoreKit.

Real examples. Large apps (Airbnb, Uber, Spotify) split the codebase into many frameworks/packages generated by Bazel, Buck, Tuist or XcodeGen to keep project.pbxproj conflicts away and builds cacheable.

Analogy. Target is the dish, configuration is the recipe variation (mild vs spicy), scheme is the order slip saying "dish X, spicy, serve at table 5".

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing configuration (settings) with scheme (what to run).
  • Not knowing Archive uses Release by default and Run uses Debug.
  • Forgetting to share a scheme, breaking CI.
  • Thinking one target per environment is required; build configurations are cheaper.

notes.title: Swift Package Manager basics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Gradle implementation("...") with Maven Central, plus include(":core") for local modules. SPM is the dependency manager built into Xcode and the Swift toolchain.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "Networking",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17), .macOS(.v14)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "Networking", targets: ["Networking"]),
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(url: "https://github.com/apple/swift-log.git", from: "1.5.0"),
        .package(path: "../Core"),                       // local package
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "Networking",
            dependencies: [
                .product(name: "Logging", package: "swift-log"),
                "Core",
            ],
            resources: [.process("Resources")]
        ),
        .testTarget(name: "NetworkingTests", dependencies: ["Networking"]),
    ],
    swiftLanguageModes: [.v6]
)
// :networking/build.gradle.kts
plugins { id("com.android.library"); kotlin("android") }
android { namespace = "com.app.networking"; defaultConfig { minSdk = 26 } }
dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.microutils:kotlin-logging:3.0.5")
    implementation(project(":core"))
    testImplementation(kotlin("test"))
}

Vocabulary.

  • Package: a directory with Package.swift. Contains targets.
  • Target: a module (source folder under Sources/<Name>), either .target, .executableTarget, .testTarget, .binaryTarget (a prebuilt XCFramework), .plugin.
  • Product: what the package exposes (.library, .executable). Consumers depend on products, not targets.
  • Dependency: a package by URL with a version rule (from:, exact:, .upToNextMinor(from:), branch:, revision:) or by path:.

Resolution. SPM writes Package.resolved (like a lockfile; commit it for apps). Resolved clones live in DerivedData and ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm. Xcode shows "Package Dependencies"; File > Packages > Reset Package Caches fixes corrupt resolution; Resolve Package Versions refreshes.

Resources and bundles. Resources in a package are accessed through Bundle.module, not Bundle.main (a classic bug when images from a package do not appear):

Image("logo", bundle: .module)
Text("title", bundle: .module)

Binary targets. Firebase and Google SDKs ship as XCFramework binary targets, which is why resolution downloads big zips (Firebase package is large, noticeable in clean-build times).

Swift settings. Per-target swiftSettings: [.enableUpcomingFeature("..."), .define("DEBUG", .when(configuration: .debug))] and unsafeFlags (not allowed for dependencies fetched by version).

Plugins. Build tool plugins (SwiftLint plugin, SwiftGen, OpenAPI generator) run during build; Xcode asks you to trust them, and CI needs -skipPackagePluginValidation/-skipMacroValidation for macros (swift-syntax based macros too).

Real examples. Point-Free (swift-composable-architecture, swift-dependencies), Apple (swift-collections, swift-async-algorithms, swift-log), Alamofire, Kingfisher, Nuke, Lottie, Firebase and Sentry all support SPM.

Analogy. A package is a boxed kit of parts with a parts list (Package.swift); a product is the finished item sold from the kit.

Common interview traps.

  • Depending on a target instead of a product from another package.
  • Using Bundle.main for package resources (must be Bundle.module).
  • Not committing Package.resolved, giving non-reproducible CI builds.
  • Using branch: in production dependencies.

notes.title: Modularization with local packages
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Multi-module Gradle with :core, :feature:home, :data, convention plugins. On iOS, local SPM packages (or Xcode framework targets) are the lightweight way to modularize.

 App target (thin: DI, navigation root, App entry)
   |-- FeatureHome  --> Core, DesignSystem
   |-- FeatureCart  --> Core, DesignSystem
   |-- Core         --> (nothing)
   |-- DesignSystem --> (nothing)
   `-- Networking   --> Core

Setup. Create a folder Packages/, add a Package.swift per package (or one multi-target package), then in Xcode drag the folder into the project (appears as a local package) and add the products to the app target's "Frameworks, Libraries, and Embedded Content". A local package referenced by path: is edited live with no resolve step.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Packages/Package.swift: one package, many targets
// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "Packages",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "Core", targets: ["Core"]),
        .library(name: "FeatureHome", targets: ["FeatureHome"]),
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "Core"),
        .target(name: "FeatureHome", dependencies: ["Core"]),
        .testTarget(name: "FeatureHomeTests", dependencies: ["FeatureHome"]),
    ]
)
// settings.gradle.kts
include(":app", ":core", ":feature:home")

// feature/home/build.gradle.kts
dependencies { implementation(project(":core")) }

Access control across modules. internal (default) is invisible to other modules; anything exposed must be public. Structs need a public init: the memberwise initializer is internal. This is the number one modularization paper-cut. package access (Swift 5.9) shares symbols across modules within the same package. open allows subclassing/overriding outside the module.

public struct Product: Sendable, Identifiable {
    public let id: UUID
    public let name: String
    public init(id: UUID, name: String) { self.id = id; self.name = name }  // required
}

Static vs dynamic linking. SPM libraries link statically by default in an app. If two dynamic frameworks both embed the same static package you get duplicate-symbol warnings and "Class X is implemented in both" at runtime. Pick type: .dynamic only deliberately (e.g. shared between app and extensions to avoid duplication). Dynamic frameworks cost launch time (dyld work); the App Store Connect / Instruments "App Launch" template shows it.

Interface/implementation split. Teams at Airbnb, Uber and Spotify use protocol-only "interface" modules so feature modules do not depend on each other's implementations, enabling parallel builds and incremental recompiles; the app target wires the concrete implementations (dependency injection, see the architecture track).

Build-time effect. Swift builds modules in parallel when the dependency graph is wide; a tall chain serializes. Changing a public API recompiles dependents; changing internals does not. Keep a small stable Core.

Pitfalls. SwiftUI previews (#Preview) in packages need the package target to be built for iOS (select an iOS destination, not "My Mac"); previews of feature modules can be slow, so some teams use a small demo app target per feature.

Real examples. Point-Free's isowords is a model open-source multi-package app; Airbnb has talked at conferences about hundreds of modules built with Buck/Bazel; Tuist generates projects from Swift manifests.

Analogy. Modules are departments in a company with a front desk (public API): other departments talk to the desk, never walk into the back office.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting public init on structs, then seeing "initializer is inaccessible due to internal protection level".
  • Circular dependencies: SPM forbids them (build error), unlike sloppy folder structure.
  • Assuming package access also crosses Xcode projects; it is per package.
  • Mixing static linking of the same code into app and extension, doubling size.

notes.title: xcconfig files and environments
notes.html:
Android equivalent. buildTypes/productFlavors with buildConfigField and resValue, or gradle.properties. iOS uses .xcconfig text files assigned to build configurations.

// Config/Base.xcconfig
PRODUCT_NAME = MyApp
SWIFT_VERSION = 6.0
IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 17.0

// Config/Debug.xcconfig
#include "Base.xcconfig"
API_BASE_URL = staging.api.example.com
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.example.myapp.dev
APP_DISPLAY_NAME = MyApp Dev
SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS = DEBUG

// Config/Release.xcconfig
#include "Base.xcconfig"
API_BASE_URL = api.example.com
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.example.myapp
APP_DISPLAY_NAME = MyApp

Note: // starts a comment in xcconfig files, so a full URL gets truncated. Store the host only and prepend https:// in code (or split the slashes with https:/$()/).

Surface the values in Info.plist, then read them in Swift.

<key>API_BASE_URL</key>
<string>$(API_BASE_URL)</string>
<key>CFBundleDisplayName</key>
<string>$(APP_DISPLAY_NAME)</string>
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum AppConfig {
    static let baseURL: URL = {
        guard let s = Bundle.main.object(forInfoDictionaryKey: "API_BASE_URL") as? String,
              let url = URL(string: "https://" + s) else {
            fatalError("API_BASE_URL missing")      // fail fast in development
        }
        return url
    }()
}
object AppConfig {
    val baseUrl: String = BuildConfig.API_BASE_URL   // buildConfigField in flavor
}

(The host-only value avoids the // comment problem.)

Wiring. Project > Info > Configurations: assign Debug.xcconfig to the Debug configuration (project-level or target-level), Release.xcconfig to Release. A Staging configuration (duplicate Release) gets Staging.xcconfig. A scheme per environment (MyApp-Staging) chooses the configuration for Run/Archive. For side-by-side installs use different PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER and app icon names (ASSETCATALOG_COMPILER_APPICON_NAME).

Compile-time flags. SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS (e.g. DEBUG STAGING) enables #if DEBUG / #if STAGING blocks. Prefer config values over scattered #if, and never ship debug menus in a Release build.

Secrets. Do not commit API secrets in xcconfig or Info.plist; the app bundle is a zip anyone can unpack, and strings finds hardcoded keys. Options: public client IDs only in xcconfig; per-user Secrets.xcconfig that is git-ignored and #include? (optional include) loaded locally and injected by CI; real secrets stay on a backend proxy; user tokens in the Keychain.

#include? "Secrets.xcconfig"

CocoaPods interplay. Pods generate their own xcconfig files; you must #include the Pods xcconfig in yours or lose pod settings ("Unable to open base configuration reference file").

Real examples. Most mature apps use xcconfig + configurations; Fastlane match and gym build lanes pass configuration:; Firebase uses different GoogleService-Info.plist per environment, copied by a Run Script phase.

Analogy. xcconfig files are labelled switchboards: flip the panel (configuration) and every light in the building (setting) changes together.

Common interview traps.

  • Writing https://... literally in xcconfig (truncated at //).
  • Putting secrets in xcconfig and assuming obfuscation.
  • Forgetting to expose a setting in Info.plist (it only exists at build time otherwise).
  • Mistaking #if DEBUG for a runtime check; it is compile-time.

notes.title: Info.plist, entitlements and capabilities
notes.html:
Android equivalent. AndroidManifest.xml holds package name, permissions (<uses-permission>), components, intent filters and <meta-data>. iOS splits this across Info.plist (metadata, usage strings, URL schemes), the entitlements file (signed capabilities), and runtime permission prompts.

Info.plist. A property list (XML) with app metadata. Since Xcode 13, new projects have no standalone Info.plist file by default; keys live in target > Info tab and build settings (GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE = YES, INFOPLIST_KEY_*), but a file is still used when you need custom/complex keys.

Key Meaning
CFBundleIdentifier Bundle id (like applicationId)
CFBundleShortVersionString Marketing version (like versionName)
CFBundleVersion Build number (like versionCode)
NSCameraUsageDescription etc. Purpose strings for permission prompts
UILaunchScreen Launch screen config
CFBundleURLTypes Custom URL schemes (deep links)
LSApplicationQueriesSchemes Schemes you may query with canOpenURL
UIBackgroundModes Background execution (audio, location, fetch, processing, remote-notification)
ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption Export compliance answer
UIApplicationSceneManifest Scene config 
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>We use the camera to scan receipts.</string>
<key>NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription</key>
<string>Show stores near you.</string>

App Store rejection pattern. Missing or vague purpose strings. Calling an API (camera, photos, location, contacts, Face ID NSFaceIDUsageDescription, tracking NSUserTrackingUsageDescription) without the key crashes the app at the call with "This app has crashed because it attempted to access privacy-sensitive data without a usage description" (the crash log shows __TCC_CRASHING_DUE_TO_PRIVACY_VIOLATION__). Apple also rejects generic strings ("needed for app"). Also add the Privacy Manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, required for apps and third-party SDKs using "required reason APIs" such as UserDefaults, file timestamps, system boot time): verify current deadlines in App Store Connect guidance.

Entitlements (MyApp.entitlements). A plist of capabilities that Apple signs into the provisioning profile; the OS enforces them.

<key>aps-environment</key>
<string>development</string>
<key>com.apple.developer.associated-domains</key>
<array><string>applinks:example.com</string></array>
<key>keychain-access-groups</key>
<array><string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)com.example.shared</string></array>
<key>com.apple.security.application-groups</key>
<array><string>group.com.example.myapp</string></array>

Capabilities tab. Adding a capability (Push Notifications, Sign in with Apple, iCloud, App Groups, Associated Domains, HealthKit, Background Modes, In-App Purchase, Apple Pay, Wallet) edits the entitlements file and updates the App ID in the developer portal; with automatic signing Xcode regenerates the provisioning profile. Mismatch produces "Provisioning profile doesn't include the ... entitlement" at archive time.

Signing in one paragraph. Certificate (Apple Development / Apple Distribution) proves identity, App ID defines bundle id + capabilities, Provisioning profile binds certificate + App ID + (for development) device UDIDs. Automatic signing (Xcode manages) is fine for solo work; CI uses Fastlane match, App Store Connect API keys, or manual signing. This replaces the Android keystore/Play App Signing model.

Share data between app and extensions. App Group container + UserDefaults(suiteName:) (widgets, share extensions); Keychain access groups for shared secrets.

Real examples. Instagram/WhatsApp-style apps declare UIBackgroundModes for VoIP/audio; ride-hailing apps use location "always" strings and have been rejected for weak wording; Sentry and Firebase SDKs ship their own PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy.

Analogy. Info.plist is the app's passport page (who I am, what I plan to do); entitlements are the visas stamped by Apple that actually permit entry.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing runtime permission alone is enough: a missing usage string crashes first.
  • Confusing CFBundleShortVersionString (user-visible) with CFBundleVersion (build, must increase per upload).
  • Thinking entitlements can be edited freely; the profile must contain them.
  • Android mix-up: iOS has no manifest-declared permissions list; prompts are driven by usage strings and runtime requests.

notes.title: Asset catalogs, string catalogs and app icons
notes.html:
Android equivalent. res/drawable, res/mipmap, res/values/strings.xml, res/values-es/strings.xml, adaptive icons, night qualifiers. iOS packs these in asset catalogs (.xcassets) and string catalogs (.xcstrings).

Asset catalog (Assets.xcassets). Contains image sets (1x/2x/3x or single vector PDF/SVG with "Preserve Vector Data"), color sets with Any/Dark appearance variants, app icon set, symbol image sets, data sets, and a launch image/color. Xcode compiles it into a Assets.car file with thinning for the target device (App Thinning, asset slicing).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
Image("hero")                          // from asset catalog
Image(systemName: "heart.fill")        // SF Symbols (built-in)
Color("BrandPrimary")                  // color set with dark variant
Color(.brandPrimary)                   // generated symbol (Xcode 15+, GENERATE_ASSET_SYMBOL_EXTENSIONS)
Image(painterResource(R.drawable.hero), contentDescription = null)
Icon(Icons.Filled.Favorite, contentDescription = null)
colorResource(R.color.brand_primary)   // night/ variant by qualifier

Xcode 15+ generates type-safe symbols (Image(.hero), Color(.brandPrimary)), removing the stringly-typed lookups that previously crashed or rendered blank at runtime when misspelled (SwiftGen and R.swift were the old fix).

App icon. Since Xcode 14, a single 1024x1024 image can be supplied ("Single Size") and Xcode derives the rest; Xcode 16 / iOS 18 adds dark and tinted variants (verify exact slots). No transparency (App Store rejects), no rounded corners (the OS masks).

Dark mode and semantic colors. Use color sets or system semantic colors (Color.primary, .secondary, UIColor.label, .systemBackground).

String catalog (Localizable.xcstrings, Xcode 15+). One JSON-backed editor for all languages, plurals ("vary by plural"), device variations, and translation state per string. Xcode auto-extracts strings from Text("..."), String(localized:) and LocalizedStringKey.

Text("welcome_title")                                       // key lookup (SwiftUI)
let msg = String(localized: "items_in_cart \(count)")        // with interpolation, plural variants in catalog
Text("Total: \(price, format: .currency(code: "USD"))")

Legacy: Localizable.strings and Localizable.stringsdict for plurals, NSLocalizedString("key", comment: ""). Right-to-left languages mirror layouts automatically for leading/trailing, not left/right.

Size and loading. Image sets from catalogs are cached by UIImage(named:) (and may be purged on memory pressure); images loaded with UIImage(contentsOfFile:) are not. Large photos in a catalog balloon the binary (App Store size limits and cellular download limit prompts, verify current cellular limit); use remote images (Kingfisher, Nuke, AsyncImage) for content.

Real examples. Airbnb and Spotify use design-system packages with their own asset catalogs and generated color tokens; SwiftGen/Tuist generate accessors for older projects.

Analogy. An asset catalog is a labelled drawer cabinet: ask for "hero" and the device receives the right size and appearance for its own screen.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Bundle.main assets from within a package (use the package bundle, see SPM section).
  • Forgetting dark variants and seeing unreadable text.
  • Putting hard-coded English strings in Swift code, so they are not extracted.
  • Submitting an icon with an alpha channel.

notes.title: CocoaPods, Carthage and why SPM won
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Like moving from manual jar management or old Maven setups to Gradle with version catalogs.

CocoaPods (legacy, Ruby). Podfile declares dependencies, pod install generates Pods/, a Podfile.lock, and an .xcworkspace you must open instead of .xcodeproj. It builds pods as static libs or frameworks (use_frameworks!), modifies your project and adds scripts. The CocoaPods team has announced the trunk is moving to read-only (verify the exact date on their blog); treat CocoaPods as maintenance-mode.

platform :ios, '17.0'
use_frameworks! :linkage => :static
target 'MyApp' do
  pod 'Alamofire', '~> 5.9'
  pod 'Kingfisher'
end

Carthage (legacy). Decentralized, builds XCFrameworks from Cartfile, you manually link them; no project mutation; slow to rebuild, little adoption now.

Aspect CocoaPods Carthage SPM
Tooling Ruby gem Binary Built into Xcode and Swift
Lockfile Podfile.lock Cartfile.resolved Package.resolved
Workspace needed Yes No No
Modifies project Yes No Xcode integration only
Binary frameworks Yes (vendored) Yes .binaryTarget
Resources Yes Yes Yes (Bundle.module)
ObjC/C Yes Yes Yes (C/ObjC/C++ targets)
Local modules Dev pods No Local packages

Why SPM won. First-party, no Ruby/Bundler, works on Linux/CI uniformly, integrated in Xcode UI, supports macros, plugins and binary targets, enables modularization without a Podspec.

Migrating off Pods. Move one library at a time: remove from Podfile, add via Xcode Package Dependencies, fix imports; libraries lacking SPM support (some ad SDKs, some Google pieces) may need .binaryTarget wrappers or the vendor's XCFramework. Coexistence is allowed.

Production incidents. pod install produced different project.pbxproj on each developer's machine; "Multiple commands produce ..." duplicate output errors; mismatched Pods lock files between CI and local; Xcode upgrades breaking pod build settings (e.g. deployment target warnings for old pods set below the project's minimum).

Real examples. Many pre-2020 apps (Uber, Lyft, Instagram) still ship with Pods or custom Buck/Bazel; new libraries ship SPM first.

Analogy. CocoaPods is a third-party moving company that rearranges your furniture; SPM is the building's own delivery dock.

Common interview traps.

  • Opening .xcodeproj instead of .xcworkspace in a Pods project, getting "No such module".
  • Mixing the same library via both Pods and SPM, causing duplicate-symbol errors.
  • Thinking Carthage is auto-integrated.
  • Claiming CocoaPods is deleted; it works but is declining.

notes.title: Build settings, DerivedData and build times
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Gradle build cache, build/ folders, configuration cache, ./gradlew clean, build scans and --profile. The Xcode analogs: DerivedData, build system settings, and the Build Timeline.

DerivedData. ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/<Project>-<hash>/ holds build products, intermediates, module caches, SwiftUI preview data, indexes, SPM checkouts (for projects). Deleting it is the "invalidate caches" of Xcode and fixes a large share of ghost errors ("Cannot find type X in scope" after a branch switch, stale module cache, phantom SourcePackages). In a separate terminal: rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData then rebuild.

Important build settings to know.

Setting Meaning
SWIFT_OPTIMIZATION_LEVEL -Onone (Debug), -O / -Osize (Release)
SWIFT_COMPILATION_MODE incremental (Debug) vs wholemodule (Release)
ONLY_ACTIVE_ARCH Build only the current arch in Debug (faster)
DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT dwarf (Debug) vs dwarf-with-dsym (Release)
ENABLE_BITCODE Removed; Bitcode deprecated since Xcode 14
IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET Minimum OS (like minSdk)
SWIFT_VERSION / SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY Language mode and checking (see the concurrency notes)
CODE_SIGN_STYLE Automatic or Manual
ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING Sandbox run-script phases
BUILD_LIBRARY_FOR_DISTRIBUTION Module stability for binary frameworks
OTHER_LDFLAGS, FRAMEWORK_SEARCH_PATHS Linker/search paths, source of many errors

Reducing build time.

  1. Measure first: Product > Perform Action > Build With Timing Summary, and the Report navigator build timeline. Add -Xfrontend -warn-long-function-bodies=200 and -warn-long-expression-type-checking=200 to OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS to find slow type-checking (long chained expressions, big literals).
  2. Modularize with a wide, shallow dependency graph; keep public API surfaces small.
  3. Debug uses incremental compile and ONLY_ACTIVE_ARCH = YES; do not use whole module in Debug.
  4. Use explicit types for large collection literals and long closures; avoid mixing numeric literals and operators in complex expressions.
  5. Avoid heavy Run Script phases in Debug; give them inputs/outputs so Xcode can skip them.
  6. Xcode 16 uses explicit modules (SWIFT_ENABLE_EXPLICIT_MODULES, verify) and a build cache; Bazel/Tuist/XCFrameworks cache prebuilt modules for large teams.
  7. Prefer @testable import only in test targets; enable "Build Active Architecture Only" in Debug.

Debugging build failures.

xcodebuild -workspace MyApp.xcworkspace -scheme MyApp -configuration Debug build 2>&1 | xcbeautify
xcodebuild -showBuildSettings -scheme MyApp | grep -i deployment
xcrun --find swift && swift --version
Error Usual cause
"No such module 'X'" Opening wrong workspace, package not resolved, target membership, missing import in module map; clean DerivedData
"Command CompileSwift failed" with no detail Open the Report navigator and expand the log; type-check timeouts show "unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time"
"Multiple commands produce" Duplicate resource names or Info.plist in Copy Bundle Resources
"Undefined symbols for architecture arm64" Missing linked framework/package product, wrong linker flags, static lib not added
"Provisioning profile ... doesn't include signing certificate" Signing mismatch; refresh in Settings > Accounts
Package resolution stuck File > Packages > Reset Package Caches; delete Package.resolved cautiously; check network/auth for private repos

Xcode shortcuts worth memorizing.

Shortcut Action
Cmd+B / Cmd+R / Cmd+U Build / Run / Test
Cmd+Shift+K Clean build folder (Cmd+Shift+Option+K deeper)
Cmd+Shift+O Open quickly (file or symbol)
Ctrl+Cmd+J / Cmd+click Jump to definition
Ctrl+I Re-indent
Cmd+Shift+L Library of views and modifiers
Cmd+Option+P Resume SwiftUI preview
Cmd+0 / Cmd+Option+0 Toggle navigator / inspector
Cmd+/ Toggle comment
Ctrl+6 Document items (jump bar symbols)
Cmd+Shift+Y Toggle debug area

Debugging tools. LLDB (po, p, expr, bt), the View Debugger and Memory Graph Debugger (Debug menu), breakpoints (exception, symbolic), Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations, Leaks, Swift Concurrency, Hangs), Organizer for crashes, hang rate, energy; MetricKit for field data.

Real examples. Teams at Airbnb and Spotify report build time tracking per commit as a CI metric; Point-Free published type-checker timing articles; Bazel with remote caching is used by large iOS orgs.

Analogy. DerivedData is a workshop's scrap and half-assembled parts bin; when odd mistakes appear, clearing the bin and starting fresh usually works.

Common interview traps.

  • Instantly blaming the code and not trying a clean DerivedData / package cache reset.
  • Not knowing Cmd+Shift+K cleans the build folder (intermediates) while deleting DerivedData also clears indexes and SPM caches.
  • Using Release settings in Debug (very slow builds) or Debug in perf measurement (misleadingly slow runs; always profile Release).
  • Thinking Bitcode is still relevant.

notes.title: Legacy and migration notes
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Like finding Groovy build.gradle, Kapt and jcenter() in an old repo: you read it, then modernize it module by module.

You will meet these in old codebases:

  • Storyboards/XIBs and AppDelegate-only lifecycle (UIApplicationMain), later the scene lifecycle (SceneDelegate); SwiftUI apps use @main struct MyApp: App.
  • Info.plist files with UIMainStoryboardFile and scene manifests copied across projects.
  • CocoaPods plus Fastlane, Gemfile, .ruby-version.
  • R.swift/SwiftGen-generated resources replaced by Xcode 15 symbols.
  • Localizable.strings replaced by string catalogs (Xcode can migrate with "Migrate to String Catalog").
  • Manual .xcodeproj merges replaced by XcodeGen/Tuist, or Xcode 16 synchronized groups (verify for your Xcode version).
  • Objective-C bridging headers (MyApp-Bridging-Header.h) for mixed-language projects; modules with Obj-C need an umbrella header and module map.
  • NavigationView and ObservableObject in app code (see SwiftUI notes).

Migration plan for an older app.

1. Set Xcode/Swift versions in CI (.xcode-version or xcodes) and pin them.
2. Introduce xcconfig; move scattered build settings out of the project UI.
3. Add SwiftLint/SwiftFormat via SPM plugin or Run Script.
4. Extract Core/DesignSystem into local packages; then feature packages.
5. Replace Pods one by one with SPM.
6. Adopt string catalogs and asset symbols.
7. Turn on strict concurrency per module (see the Swift 6 concurrency note).

Analogy. Migration is replacing the wiring in a house room by room while living in it.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing a "big bang" rewrite of the build system; incremental modularization is the senior answer.
  • Not mentioning CI pinning of Xcode versions (different Xcode builds the same code differently).
  • Forgetting that changing the deployment target changes available APIs (@available, #available).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Xcode concepts: workspace (container), project, target (product), configuration (settings set), scheme (what to run with which configuration). Share schemes for CI.
  • SPM is the default: Package.swift, products vs targets, version rules, Package.resolved, Bundle.module for resources, binary targets, plugins.
  • Modularize with local packages: public APIs and public init, no cycles, wide shallow graph, static linking by default, package access within a package.
  • xcconfig per configuration drives environments (bundle id, base URL, flags); surface through Info.plist; avoid // in URLs; never put secrets in the bundle.
  • Info.plist holds metadata and purpose strings; entitlements are signed capabilities in the provisioning profile; missing usage strings crash; add privacy manifests (verify policy).
  • Asset catalogs (symbols, dark variants, single-size icon) and string catalogs replace res/.
  • CocoaPods and Carthage are legacy; migrate to SPM incrementally.
  • Fix weird builds with DerivedData / package cache resets; measure build time with timing summary and type-check warnings; profile only Release builds.
  • Know the shortcuts and tools: Cmd+B/R/U, Cmd+Shift+K, Cmd+Shift+O, LLDB, Instruments, Organizer.
